div.head: Diet and Population Genomics of River Otters (Lontra canadensis) in West Virginia
Eden Grace Nitza
div.p: North American river otters (Lontra canadensis), hereafter, otters, are apex predators in aquatic ecosystems across Appalachia, and thus have important impacts on their ecosystems such as food web regulation, nutrient cycling, and reducing the impacts of invasive species. Otters were extirpated from most of Appalachia, including all of West Virginia, by the mid -1900's due to habitat destruction and overharvest. The West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR) began an otter reintroduction program in 1984 which translocated approximately 250 otters into the state by 1997. This reintroduction program was largely considered successful, and a regulated harvest season was opened in 2011. Despite these successes, challenges to otter conservation and management in West Virginia persist. The WVDNR Wildlife Resources Section is responsible for managing wildlife and fish populations at sustainable levels, and as such, has identified two main challenges facing contemporary otter conservation and management: human-wildlife conflict and a lack of understanding regarding the population genomic impacts of the reintroduction program. This thesis was aimed at addressing both challenges. In chapter 1, I addressed human-otter conflict. Otter recovery has been complicated by concern that they consume stocked trout (Oncorhynchus sp., Salmo sp., and Salvelinus sp.) to an extent that is economically harmful to West Virginians. To address this issue, I conducted a multilocus DNA metabarcoding assessment of otter stomach contents (n=86) collected from licensed trappers and as roadkill from 2020-2023 to determine diet composition of otters across West Virginia. This is the first study to utilize DNA metabarcoding to assess both vertebrate and invertebrate otter diet. I found that the most common diet items were fish in the family Centrarchidae (sunfishes) and invertebrates in the family Cambaridae (crayfish). Trout occurred in only 10% of sampled otter stomachs. No differences in diet composition were observed according to age, sex, or year. These data will be used to assess the extent to which an increase in otter harvest is an appropriate management strategy for otters in West Virginia. In chapter 2, I addressed the lack of understanding regarding the population genomic impacts of the reintroduction program. I amalgamated otter tissue samples (n=395) collected from 2006-2023 from across several U.S. Appalachian states in which otters were reintroduced (Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia) as well as from the two primary source states for the reintroductions (Louisiana and North Carolina). I analyzed 13,468 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) using a double digest restriction-site (ddRAD) method. These results indicated that two genetically defined populations are present across Appalachia (K=2); western Ohio was genetically differentiated from the rest of the study area. Virginia and West Virginia's populations had lower genome-wide heterozygosity measures than the source states and effective population sizes were low across the study area (Ne < 500). These data will guide conservation decision-makers as to how we can best ensure the long-term persistence of this species. These results are also informative as to Appalachian ecosystem recovery progress.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Worldwide, thirteen extant species of otters are recognized by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (Duplaix and Savage 2018). Otters are members of the weasel family, Mustilidae, and occupy aquatic and semi-aquatic ecosystems on all continents except Australia and Antarctica. All otter species are generalist carnivores that often function as apex predators in a wide range of habitats, and as such, they play an important role in ecosystem function and regulation. In North America, two species of otters are found: the sea otter (Enhydra lutris), which occupies exclusively marine ecosystems off the Pacific coast, and the North American river otter (Lontra canadensis), which occupies freshwater, estuarine, and marine ecosystems across the continent (Duplaix and Savage 2018).

The North American river otter (hereafter, otter) was historically present in all major North American watersheds except for the extremities of the Southwestern desert and the Arctic tundra (Hall, 1981;Melquist & Dronkert 1987). However, the onset of European colonization resulted in the unsustainable harvest of otters for their fur; by the nineteenth century, they were one of the most important species in the global fur trade (Schorger 1970, Toweill andTabor 1982). European colonization also brought habitat destruction, which, in synergy with overharvest, led to severe population declines across their historic range. Water pollution, specifically sedimentation and run-off from industrialization and agriculture, as well as anthropogenic alterations of aquatic ecosystems such as channelization, damming, and wetland drainage, are thought to be the main contributors to the destruction of suitable otter habitat (Bottorff et al 1976, Toweill and Tabor 1982, Melquist and Dronkert 1987). By the early twentieth century, otters had been extirpated or greatly reduced from most of their range (Toweill andTabor 1982, Melquist andDronkert 1987). Otter population declines were most severe in the inland United States, which is attributed to these habitats both naturally supporting less diverse and abundant aquatic ecosystems and more intense habitat destruction compared to coastal areas (Melquist and Dronkert 1987, Melquist et al. 2003, Bricker et al. 2022). By the mid-1900s, the range of the otter had been reduced to less than 75% of its historic extent (Melquist et al. 2003) and had been extirpated or nearly extirpated from Arizona, Colorado, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Nebraska, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, and West Virginia (Park 1971).

Despite management issues in the past, contemporarily otters are considered a conservation success story. As of 2018, they are listed as "Least Concern" by the IUCN red list and occupy approximately 90% of their historic, pre-European colonization range across what is now the United States (Duplaix and Savage 2018). As of 2016, otters occupy at least portions of every U.S. state, province, and territory within their historic range (Roberts et al. 2020 andBricker et al. 2022) and none of these areas reported declining population trends (Bricker et al. 2022). This recovery is the result of a synergy of conservation actions that began in the 1970's, namely human-mediated reintroduction programs, watershed restoration, and the implementation of managed harvests (Raesly 2001, Melquist et al. 2003). Twenty-two states across the U.S.

implemented otter reintroduction programs (Bricker et al. 2022), which in total translocated approximately 4,000 otters between 1976 and 1998, most of which were sourced from Louisiana (Erb et al 2018). Additionally, the implementation of the federal Clean Water Act in 1972 and the listing of the North American river otter under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in 1977 are considered critical contributions to otter recovery (Raesly 2001, Melquist et al. 2003, Bricker et al. 2022).

In West Virginia, river otters were extirpated by the mid -1900's due to habitat destruction and overharvesting. The last known West Virginia otter to have been trapped prior to its complete extirpation in the state was in the mid-1950's in Tucker County, but they had been considered rare across the state since the early 1900's (Bottorf et al. 1976). The destruction of suitable habitat for otters in this area was caused specifically by logging, uncontrolled wildfires, and agricultural practices. However, as with much of the country, the 1970's brought a wave of ecosystem restoration efforts to West Virginia, including forest management, prescribed burning, and improved agricultural practices (Bottorf et al. 1976). In 1976, the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR), the state's wildlife agency, conducted a river otter restoration feasibility study that concluded the state could once again support an otter population due to extensive habitat restoration and a halt on harvest (Bottorff et al. 1976).

The WVDNR thus began an otter reintroduction program in 1984 (Bricker et al. 2022, Roberts et al. 2022), with the anticipated benefits of this reintroduction being primarily aesthetics and harvest (Bottorf et al. 1976 Despite these successes, challenges to otter conservation and management in West Virginia persist. The WVDNR Wildlife Resources Section is responsible for managing wildlife and fish populations at sustainable levels, and as such, has identified two main challenges facing contemporary otter conservation and management: human-wildlife conflict and a lack of understanding regarding the population genomic impacts of the reintroduction program. Humanotter conflict has been identified as an issue because of a concern that otters diminish populations of game fish, particularly Salmonids (trout), to an extent that is economically harmful (Melquist et al. 2003, Serfass et al. 2014), which has been identified as a more pressing issue in central U.S. states in which more otters were reintroduced than elsewhere in North America (Bricker et al. 2022). This challenge has persisted since before the reintroduction program; in 1976, the main concern of the WVDNR in regards to a river otter reintroduction program was "social problems" (Bottorf 1976).

Additionally, although the otter population in West Virginia is considered recovered from a demographic perspective, the impact of the reintroduction program on its population genomics is unknown (Bricker et al. 2022). An understanding of contemporary population genomics patterns could thus aid in the conservation and management of this population (Bricker et al. 2022). Population genomics are an important management tool for reintroduced populations (DeYoung and Honeycut 2005) as they can be representative of overall fitness and long-term adaptive potential of a population (Lacy 1997, Reed andFrankham 2003). Reintroduced populations are also threatened by the potential negative effects of reintroductions, such as founder effects and outbreeding depression, which can threaten the long-term persistence of reintroduced populations (Armstrong and Seddon 2008).

The overall objective of this thesis is to assess the diet and population genomic structure and diversity of otters across West Virginia, USA. This research will be utilized to assess if otter harvest regulations in West Virginia should be adjusted to mitigate the potential negative impact of otters on the sport-fishing industry.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although apex predators are known to serve critical regulatory roles in their ecosystems (Estes et al. 2011, Soule et al. 2003, Sergio et al. 2008,), their conservation and management is often complicated by human-predator conflict over shared resources, whether that conflict is realized or perceived (Ripple et al. 2014). North American river otters (Lontra canadensis), hereafter, otters, are apex predators in aquatic ecosystems across Appalachia, and thus have important impacts on their ecosystems such as food web regulation, nutrient cycling, and reducing the impacts of invasive species (Hammerschlag et al. 2019). Otters are known to be critical links between aquatic and terrestrial nitrogen cycling, which causes an increase in plant growth in terrestrial riparian areas in which otters are present compared to areas where otters are not present (Crait and Ben-David, 2007). Although otters were extirpated from extensive regions of the inland United States by the mid-1900's due to habitat destruction and overharvest (Hall, 1981;Toweill andTabor 1982, Melquist &Dronkert 1987), extensive conservation actions such as water quality legislation, habitat restoration, and reintroduction programs have allowed otters to recover to nearly 90% of their native range as of 2018 (Duplaix and Savage 2018, Roberts et al. 2020, Bricker et al. 2022).

However, this recovery has not been entirely supported by communities in which otters have returned. The purported conflict between humans and otters is centered around the perception that otters consume quantities of game fish, particularly Salmonids (trout and salmon)

to an extent that is detrimental to the angling community (Lagler and Ostenson, 1942, Serfass et al. 2014, Pearce et al. 2017). This conflict was documented as early as 1942 in Michigan in response to an increase in otter populations as a result of a moratorium on harvest (Lagler and Ostenson, 1942). The angling community called for reopening of an otter harvest season, and to address this, an otter diet study was conducted. Upon examining otter digestive tracts with microscopy, this study concluded that game fishes were not the most common diet item and that non-game, forage fishes (suckers, minnows, etc.) were most likely preferred by otters (Lagler and Ostenson 1942).

Despite this research, human-otter conflict has continued to present a challenge to wildlife management agencies. Unfortunately, this conflict has been erroneously inflated in media accounts, especially in areas in which reintroduction programs occurred, which has perpetuated the perceived conflict (Serfass et al. 2014, Pearce et al. 2017, Bricker et al. 2022).

Since 1942, numerous studies have examined otter diet composition with the intent of addressing conflict between people and otters (Sheldon and Toll 1964, Knudsen and Hale 1968, Toweill and Tabor 1982, Manning et al. 1990, Heenkenda et al. 2023, Sanders et al. 2023). This research has established that otters are generalist carnivores with fish and crayfish constituting the majority of their diet (Sheldon andToll 1964, Reid et al. 1994). Evidence suggests that otters consume fish species in direct proportion to their abundance and in inverse proportion to the relative agility of the species available in accordance with optimal foraging theory (Ryder 1955, Toweill and Tabor 1982, Melquist and Dronkert 1987). Most published research supports the hypothesis that otters select for slow-moving fish species such as those in the family Centrarchidae (sunfishes) (Sheldon and Toll 1964, Barding and Lacki 2012, Dekar et al. 2015). Other fish families commonly reported as major otter diet items include Cyprinidae (Reid et al. 1994),
Catostomidae, and Clupeidae (Heun et al. 2022).

Conclusions on the extent to which fast-moving fish such as Salmonids (trout and salmon) are consumed by otters in systems with known populations of Salmonids are varied. Sheldon and Toll (1964) reported no consumption of lake (Salvelinus namaycush), brown (Salmo trutta), or rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in a reservoir in central Massachusetts, USA with known populations of those trout species. Reid et al. (1994) reported no consumption of lake trout with known populations of lake trout in northeastern Alberta, Canada. Recent research has concluded that trout species were not a major component of otter diets in Indiana (Heenkenda et al. 2023) or in North Carolina (Sanders et al. 2023). Conversely, brown trout was found to be a main diet item in northern California, USA (Manning 1990) and Utah, USA (Day et al. 2015).

Although otter diet studies tend to focus on fish prey items, some research suggests that otter diet patterns are more dependent on invertebrate prey availability (primarily crayfish) than on fish availability (Dekar et al. 2010, Heun et al, 2022). Typically, otter consumption of crayfish is highest in the summer and lowest in the winter (Sheldon andToll 1964, Reid et al. 1994). However, Dekar et al. (2010) concluded that crayfish are major prey items when available (typically only in the summer), and that fish consumption increases in the winter months not because of a preference for fish but because of a decrease in the availability of crayfish. Crayfish have also been found to be more common in otter diets than fish in some systems (a river valley in Arizona, USA, Taylor et al. 2003, riparian systems in Wisconsin, USA, Heun et al. 2022).

As otters are a generalist carnivore, their diet patterns can vary greatly depending on seasons (Dekar et al. 2010), habitat characteristics (Day et al. 2015, Fretueg et al. 2015, Sanders et al. 2023), prey availability (Toweill and Tabor 1982, Melquist and Dronkert 1987, Day et al. 2015), and even individual otters (Heenkenda et al. 2023). Otters are opportunistic predators, and as such, will take advantage of even unexpected diet items, including snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus), red-shouldered hawk (Buteo lineatus) (Lagler and Ostenson, 1942), and blueberries (Vaccinium sect. Cyanococcus) (Sheldon and Toll 1982). An understanding of local-scale otter diet is important for conservation management because otter consumption of prey species can represent a significant portion of prey production, and thus otters are considered to have significant trophic effects in aquatic ecosystems (Kruuk et al. 1993, Dekar et al. 2010, Hammerschlag et al. 2019).

Previous studies on otter diet have also been mostly limited in methodology to microscopy, which is known to underestimate prey species assemblages compared to alternative methodologies, including fatty acid analysis, stable isotope analysis, and DNA metabarcoding (Satterthwaite-Phillips et al. 2014, Berry et al. 2015). Before these alternative, more robust methodologies had been applied to river otter diet investigations, soft-bodied prey, including mollusks and amphibians, were not considered to be main prey items for otters. However, the first study to apply fatty acid analysis to an otter diet investigation reported mollusks and amphibians as main diet items, with mollusks constituting 32% of otter diet in Illinois, USA 2023) also determined that otter diet composition varies significantly across physiographic regions. However, neither study was successful in utilizing DNA metabarcoding to determine invertebrate otter diet items (Heenkenda et al. 2023, Sanders et al. 2023), despite their known importance in otter diet (Taylor et al. 2003, Dekar et al. 2010, and Heun et al. 2022). Thus, to date, DNA metabarcoding has not been utilized to assess comprehensive L. canadensis diet composition, but this method has demonstrated the capacity to inform wildlife managers as to the extent to which otters depredate upon game fish compared to nongame fishes. Given that otter diet studies have been used to inform harvest regulations in the past (Lagler andOstenson, 1942, Knudsen andHale 1968), and that overharvest has historically caused widespread otter extirpations (Toweill andTabor 1982, Melquist andDronkert 1987), an understanding of the frequency and percent occurrence of all otter diet items at the local scale is necessary for the proper management and conservation of this species.

Otter diet composition has yet to be studied in West Virginia and, given the extent to which otter diet varies regionally, conclusions about otter diet in West Virginia based on otter diet elsewhere should be cautioned.

To address this issue, in this chapter I evaluated comprehensive otter diet composition across West Virginia, USA using multilocus DNA metabarcoding. This research provided valuable estimates of otter diet composition, including frequency of occurrences of vertebrate and invertebrate prey. Wildlife managers will be informed as to the extent to which otters in West Virginia are depredating upon gamefish, most importantly, stocked species of trout, including brown trout (Salmo trutta), rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), and brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis), so that appropriate decisions can be made on how to balance the needs of ecosystem conservation and human uses. This was also the first study to include invertebrate prey items within a DNA metabarcoding approach, which was informative as to the importance of this prey resource for this species overall. This research contributes to the long-term goal of conserving West Virginia's reintroduced river otter population for both the purposes of ecological functioning (as apex predators) and as a resource for human uses (as a trapped furbearer) while mitigating any detrimental impacts from depredation of trout species to the sportfishing community. I hypothesized that perceived human-otter conflict (otters consuming trout in proportions that are detrimental to the game-fishing industry) is not supported by diet analysis of otters in West Virginia. If perceived human-otter conflict is not supported by diet analysis, trout would not have been a major diet item compared to other fish or invertebrates. I formulated this hypothesis based on published research on otter diet and human-otter conflict studies, both of which suggest that otters do not meaningfully impact the sport-fishing industry (Lagler and Ostenson 1942, Sheldon and Toll 1964, Knudsen and Hale 1968, Reid et al. 1994, Pearce et al. 2017, Heenkenda 2023, Sanders 2023) and that human-otter conflict is erroneously inflated in media accounts (Serfass et al. 2014, Pearce et al. 2017, Bricker et al. 2022).

div.head: DNA Extraction
div.p: The 10mL stomach subsample was then thawed completely and further sub-sampled by removing 400μL with a wide-bore pipette tip. The 400μL sub-sample was vacuum-concentrated for 30 minutes without heat using a Savant DNA 120 SpeedVac Concentrator (Thermo Scientific Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) to improve DNA yield. Genomic DNA was then extracted using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions and eluted in 100µL. Extraction negatives were included in each batch of extractions to manage contamination. All DNA extractions were performed in a lab dedicated to sensitive analysis. The concentration and quality of the extractions were determined using a NanoDrop
One Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and normalized to 10ng/μL.

div.head: Design of Otter Blocking PNA Clamp
div.p: To block the amplification of otter DNA, I utilized a custom peptide nucleic acid (PNA) clamp, which is a synthetic, single-stranded sequence of DNA that is bound to a peptide backbone (Eriksson and Neilson, 1996). This PNA clamp was designed by PNA Bio (Thousand Oaks, California, USA) to block the amplification of otter DNA while not reducing the amplification of potential prey species or closely related species by the vertebrate primer set 12SV5 (Riaz et al. 2011). I utilized a PNA clamp because I was unsuccessful in developing a reliable otter-blocking primer probe using common methodologies (Vestheim and Jarman 2008, Kumari et al., 2019, Swinehart et al. 2023). Previous studies have successfully developed and implemented PNA clamps to prevent the amplification of host DNA in diet metabarcoding studies (Terahara et al. 2011, Homma et al. 2022). I determined that the PNA clamp was successful in blocking otter DNA but not potential prey species by comparing amplification of otter DNA to amplification of prey species with and without the PNA clamp. The PCR conditions for this reaction were as follows: 12.5μL 2X Qiagen Plus Multiplex Master Mix (Qiagen), 0.5μL of 10μM 12SV5 Forward, 0.5μL of 10μM 12SV5 Reverse, 1.25μL of 5μM PNA clamp (not included in reactions without the clamp), 1.0μL of 10ng/μL template DNA extract, brought to 25μL total reaction volume with PCR water. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: 95°C for 3 minutes for initial denaturation, followed by 30 cycles of 94°C for 20 s, 70°C

for 20 s, 57°C for 20 s, 68°C for 20 s for annealing, and then after the 30 cycles, 68°C for 10 min for final extension. A 1% agarose gel was used to determine to what extent amplification occurred. The PNA clamp was considered successful when no band could be seen from the reaction with otter DNA and the PNA clamp and when there were visible bands from the following reactions: otter without PNA clamp, prey species with clamp, and prey species without clamp.

div.head: Prey amplification, Library Preparation, and Sequencing
div.p: Prey DNA was amplified from the stomach DNA extracts using four primer sets (Table 1). Because otters are generalist species and known to consume a diverse assemblage of species, primers were selected with the intention of being able to amplify the full assemblage of potential prey species. In summary, primer sets 12SV5 (Riaz et al. 2011) and AcMDB07 (Bylemans et al. 2018) were selected to amplify potential vertebrate prey species sequences (AcMDB07 primarily amplifies fish), while primer sets BF1_BR2-COI (Elbrecht & Leese 2017) and MiDeca (Komai et al. 2017) were selected to amplify potential invertebrate prey species sequences (MiDeca primarily amplifies crayfish). All primers were adjusted to include overhang sequences, which allowed for compatibility with Illumina sequencing adapters. As primer set 12SV5 was the only primer set likely to amplify host DNA, the PNA clamp was only used in combination with 12SV5. The PCR conditions for primer set 12SV5 and the PNA clamp were as follows: 12.5μL

2X Qiagen Plus Multiplex Master Mix (Qiagen), 0.5μL of 10μM 12SV5 F, 0.5μL of 10μM 12SV5 R, 1.25μL of 5μM PNA clamp, 1.0μL of 10ng/μL template DNA extract, brought to 25μL total reaction volume with PCR water. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows:

95°C for 3 minutes for initial denaturation, followed by 30 cycles of 94°C for 20 s, 70°C for 20 s, 57°C for 20 s, 68°C for 20 s for annealing, and then after the 30 cycles, 68°C for 10 min for final extension. For primer sets AcMDB07, BF1_BR2-COI, and MiDeca, each PCR consisted of the following: 5μL 2X Qiagen Plus Multiplex Master Mix (Qiagen), 1μL of 0.02μM forward and reverse primer mix, 2μL of 10ng/μL template DNA, brought to 10μL total reaction volume with PCR water. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: 95°C for 15 min for initial denaturation, 30 cycles of 94°C for 30 s, 57°C for 90 s, and 72 °C for 1 min for annealing, and then 60°C for 30 min for final extension. PCR negatives were included in all batches of PCRs to assess contamination. Genotyping-in-thousands by sequencing (GT-seq) was then performed to sequence amplicons from the PCR reactions. Library preparation was performed with a methodology adapted from Campbell et al. (2015). A barcoding PCR was performed to label each sample with an identifiable sequence. Each PCR consisted of the following: 1.0μL of 10μM i07 index (unique to each 96-well plate), 5.0μL of Qiagen Plus Multiplex Master Mix (Qiagen), 2μL of 5μM i05 barcode (unique to each sample on each plate), and 2μL of diluted (dilution factor of 13.33) PCR DNA. The barcoding PCR thermal cycling conditions were as follows:

95°C for 15 min for initial denaturation, 10 cycles of 95°C for 10 s, 65°C for 30s, and 72°C for 30 sec for annealing, and then 72°C for 5 min for final extension. The PCR product was then normalized using a SequalPrep™ Normalization Plate Kit (ThermoFisher Scientific) and pooled. Pooled library preparation was then purified using a ThermoScientific GeneJET PCR Purification Kit. No size selection was performed because of the range of amplicon sizes across the different primer sets. Single-end sequencing of amplicons ranging from approximately 100-450 base pairs was performed on an Illumina MiSeq (Illumina, Inc., San Diego, California, USA) at the West Virginia University Genomics Core Facility.

div.head: Sequence Data Analysis
div.p: Raw sequence files were demultiplexed based on individual barcodes for each stomach and adapter sequences were removed from all sequences. Cutadapt was used to remove the primer sequence from all samples (Martin, 2011). The package OBI-Tools (Boyer et al. 2015) was used for filtering DNA sequences. Unique sequences were identified using obiuniq, reads with less than 20 occurrences and any reads shorter than 80 bp were removed using obigrep, and then PCR errors were removed using obiclean (r > 0.05). Sequences were taxonomically assigned using the BLAST plug-in with a minimum evalue of 1 e-20 and minimum identification of 98%. Sequences were assigned at the genus level. If a sequence was assigned to a genus that did not regionally occur, it was removed from the analysis. For invertebrate prey, taxa other than freshwater mussels and crayfish were removed from the analysis because they were assumed to be secondary or involuntary prey (Reid et al. 1994).

To further control for contamination, if sequences in any given sample were less than the number of sequences of that species within the extraction or PCR negative control samples, those sequences were removed from the analysis. A frequency of occurrence (FOO, the proportion of all samples in which a diet item occurred) was then constructed from the filtered data for each prey item across individual all samples. To increase confidence in our results, vertebrate diet items were then further filtered so that they were only considered present in a sample if they occurred in both sets of vertebrate primers (12SV5 and AcMDB07).

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: All statistical analyses were performed in R 4.2.2 (R Core 1). The 'type of trap' covariate was limited to foothold or body grip trap. This covariate was included because of the difference in time an otter spends in each trap type. In a body grip trap, otters are killed instantly, whereas in a foothold, otters may remain alive in the trap up to the legal limit of 24 hours. I included this covariate to ensure that any differences in diet composition across individuals were not representative of the differences between these sample types. The 'year of harvest/collection' covariate was limited to years from which I had at least five individuals. To assess if the presence or absence of Salmonid prey items in otter diet was related to age, ecoregion, or sex, I performed a logistic regression analysis. For all analyses, I assessed significance based on an α value of 0.5

div.head: Summary of Sequence Data
div.p: I obtained 44,302,050 raw, demultiplexed sequence reads from the Illumina MiSeq (Illumina), summarized by each primer set in Table 1. Using the OBI-Tools pipeline, these sequences were reduced to 19,106 molecular operational taxonomic units (MOTUs) across all primer sets. From 19,106 MOTUs, 14,544 were successfully assigned to a taxon. Corroborated results from the two vertebrate primers are provided in Appendix I. Of the 2,247 MOTUs successfully assigned to a taxon from the invertebrate primer set BF1_BR2-COI, the majority (76%) were either otter DNA (37%) or fish DNA (non-target DNA for this primer set, 38%), and thus the results from this primer were omitted from further analysis.

div.head: Performance of PNA Clamp
div.p: The PNA clamp was only utilized in conjunction with the 12SV5 primer set, which is designed to amplify all vertebrate DNA. The PNA clamp was not used with the other primer sets as those sets were not anticipated to amplify host DNA. The custom PNA clamp successfully blocked the amplification of host DNA in 56% of otter stomachs within the 12SV5 primer reactions. Of the stomachs in which host DNA was amplified, only one of those stomachs had no other prey items identified. This stomach had a relative digestion score of 4, indicating that the stomach had only liquid components.

div.head: Diet Composition of River Otters in West Virginia
div.p: From the 86 otter stomachs sampled, 75 (87%) contained at least one identifiable prey item with an average of 2.6 prey items (at the genus level) per stomach (range=0-8). Diet items consisted of fish (28 genera, 10 families), crayfish (4 genera, 1 family), herpetofauna (1 genus, 1 family), and birds (1 genus, 1 family). Sixty-four stomachs (74%) contained at least one fish genus, 43 stomachs (50%) contained at least one crayfish genus, 2 stomachs (2%) contained one herpetofauna genus, and 2 stomachs (2%) contained one avian genus. The most frequent diet items by family were Centrarchidae (sunfishes, 51%), Cambaridae (crustaceans, 50%), and Leuciscidae (minnows, 22%) (Figure 4). The most frequent genera of fish across all sampled stomachs was Lepomis (37%) followed by Micropterus (19%) and Cottus (16%) (Figure 2). The most frequent genera of crayfish across all sampled stomachs was Faxonius (41%) followed by Procambarus (9%) and Cambarus (8%) (Figure 3). All herpetofauna diet items were of a single species, the American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus). All avian diet items were of a single species, the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus). No significant differences were observed in otter diet composition based on age (p=0.215), ecoregion (p=0.4), nuisance/nonnuisance removal (p=0.851), relative digestion score (p=0.327), sex (p=0.783), type of trap (p=0.844), or year of harvest (p=0.818).

div.head: Salmonids in Otter Diet
div.p: Of the 86 otter stomachs sampled, 9 (10%) contained fish belonging to the family Salmonidae. Of those 9 stomachs, 5 (6%) contained the genus Oncorhynchus and 4 (5%) contained the genus Salvelinus. No stomachs contained fish from the genus Salmo and no stomachs contained fish from more than one genus of Salmonidae. All of the 9 stomachs that contained fish belonging to Salmonidae also contained other diet items (no stomachs had only Salmonidae). Of the 9 otters that contained Salmonidae, 4 were harvested with a nuisance permit, 4 were of unknown collection type, and 1 was roadkill. No significant differences were observed in the presence or absence of Salmonids in otter stomach samples based on age (p=0.64), ecoregion (p=0.87), or sex (p=0.48).

div.head: Otter Diet Composition
div.p: Our data provide evidence that Centrarchidae (sunfishes) and Cambaridae (freshwater crayfish) are the most frequently consumed prey items by otters in West Virginia, which is in accordance with previous research (Sheldon and Toll 1964, Barding and Lacki 2012, Dekar et al. 2015, Sanders et al. 2023). The third most frequent diet item was fish in the family Leuciscidae (true minnows). Although some of these occurrences may represent secondary prey (the prey of the prey), some studies have found primary consumption of minnows to be a major contributor to otter diet (Lagler andOstenson 1942, Melquist andHornocker 1983). Whether primary or secondary prey, minnows are contributing to otter diet. Unexpectedly, domestic chickens (Gallus gallus) were observed in two (2%) sampled otter stomachs. Although it is possible that otters did depredate upon domestic chickens, I suspect that chicken meat was used as bait to capture these individuals, which is legal and commonplace in West Virginia.

Our study did not find any significant relationships between otter diet composition and ecoregion. This conclusion is not in accordance with previous research that has found otter diet composition to vary in response to habitat characteristics (Day et al. 2015, Fretueg et al. 2015, Sanders et al. 2023). However, Day et al. (2015) defined habitat characteristics in Utah as 'order of stream', which is a finer-scale assessment of habitat than I was able to make and thus not comparable to our assessment of level III ecoregions. Fretueg et al. (2015) attributed differences in diet compared to habitat characteristics to the presence versus absence of beavers in those habitats, which I was also unable to measure. Sanders et al. (2023) found otter diet in North Carolina to vary according to physiographic regions (defined as mountains, piedmont, and coastal plain). This is an unexpected difference from our study given that the scale of physiographic regions appears similar to our scale of level III ecoregion (western Allegheny plateau, central Appalachians, ridge and valley, and blue ridge; Figure 1). Potentially, the level III ecoregions in West Virginia do not represent a diversity of habitat or prey availability to an extent that would drive differences in otter diet composition. Unfortunately, our data were limited in location to the county scale, so any further assessment of relationships between diet and habitat is not possible.

Our study also did not find any significant relationship between otter diet composition and age, sex, or year of harvest/collection. These results are in agreement with Barding and Lacki (2012), although Sanders et al. (2023) did find a significant relationship between diet composition and sex. Although I did not find any significant relationships driving otter diet composition, I suspect that otter diet composition is not random, but instead related to factors beyond the scope of this study (primarily, prey availability). Prey availability has been found to be the primary driver of otter diet composition elsewhere (Ryder 1955, Toweill and Tabor 1982, Melquist and Dronkert 1987, Day et al. 2015).

Our study is also limited in that otter stomach samples were only collected between October and May. In West Virginia, this timeframe fails to capture all seasonal differences throughout the year. Otter diet is known to shift in response to seasons with the predominant pattern being that otters consume less fish and more crayfish in the summer months when crayfish are more available (Dekar et al. 2010, Day et al. 2015). Our study is not able to assess year-round otter diet, and thus future studies should investigate sampling methods that allow for seasonal variation to be assessed.

div.head: DNA Metabarcoding to Assess Otter Diet Composition
div.p: I conclude that the methods presented here were successful in determining otter diet composition from liquid stomach contents. Otter diet composition patterns observed here are in accordance with the majority of previous research (Sheldon and Toll 1964, Barding and Lacki 2012, Dekar et al. 2015, Sanders et al. 2023). Additionally, I found no significant relationship between otter diet composition and type of trap or relative digestion score, which were utilized as measures of sample quality. Because of the differences in type of trap (body gripper or foothold), the stomach samples varied in terms of volume of stomach content. Upon dissection, stomach samples also varied in terms of degradation. I therefore interpret the lack of statistical significance between diet composition and type of trap or relative digestion score to indicate that this method was robust in identifying prey items from stomach contents regardless of relative stomach content quality.

Primers 12SV5 and AcMDB07 were successful in determining the fish components of otter diet in West Virginia. Although AcMDB07 is designed to amplify Actinopterygii (rayfinned fishes), this primer also amplified the DNA of American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus) and domestic chicken (Gallus gallus) in addition to 28 genera of fishes across 74% of sampled stomachs. The PNA clamp successfully blocked otter amplification in most (56%) of the sampled stomachs. However, as I decided to only consider prey items that were amplified by both vertebrate primers used, 12SV5 and AcMDB07, our otter diet composition results do not include potential vertebrate prey that were not amplified by AcMDB07. These potential prey items include mammals as well as other herpetofauna and birds, but these prey taxa are known to be minor contributors to otter diet (Sheldon andToll 1964, Reid et al. 1994).

Our study is the first to successfully amplify invertebrate prey items from otter stomach samples using DNA metabarcoding. These data indicate that crayfish are a major prey item for otters (occurring in 50% of all sampled stomachs), even in the winter when they are most likely less available than in other seasons (Roberts et al. 2003, Day et al. 2015). The primer set MiDeca was successful in identifying invertebrate prey items in the family Cambaridae (freshwater crayfish) including four genera of crayfish from 50% of sampled stomachs. I recommend this primer for future research on otter diet composition. However, this primer is not likely to amplify freshwater mussels. Previous research has identified freshwater mussels as an important invertebrate prey item that is often underestimated in traditional microscopy studies of otter diet (Satterwaite-Phillips 2014). Although the primer set BF1_BR2-COI was likely to amplify freshwater mussel DNA, this primer was unsuccessful because of the extent to which it amplified non-target taxon (76% of the molecular operational taxonomic units were either otter DNA or fish DNA). This primer is thus not an appropriate primer for the identification of otter invertebrate prey composition. Future research should seek to include primer sets that can amplify mollusks to better estimate both vertebrate and invertebrate prey items of otters.

div.head: Human-Otter Conflict
div.p: I conclude that in West Virginia, Salmonids are not widely consumed by otters (frequency of occurrence=10%, n=9/86). Nearly half (44%) of these otters were harvested as nuisance individuals, which indicates that the nuisance program in West Virginia successfully addresses a notable portion of the human-otter conflict. Additionally, the probability of occurrence of trout in an otter's diet was not significantly related to age, ecoregion, or sex, which I interpret to indicate that the consumption of Salmonids by otters is not related to a specific demographic of otter in West Virginia. Our results suggest that the consumption of stocked trout by otters is not commonplace and instead occurs under specific circumstances, potentially including commercial fish hatcheries and private ponds.

Our conclusion that Salmonids are not widely consumed by otters and that otters instead prefer non-game fishes is supported by the majority of previous research (Lagler and Ostenson 1942, Sheldon and Toll 1964, Knudsen and Hale 1968, Reid et al. 1994, Pearce et al. 2017, Heenkenda 2023, Sanders 2023). Some research cautions that population-wide predator control programs or an increase in harvest are not appropriate measures to address human-otter conflict because of their naturally low population densities, slow reproductive rates, and historic extirpations which are partially attributed to overharvest (Knudsen andHale 1968, Bricker et al. 2022). However, otters do consume stocked trout to an extent that is economically harmful in specific situations such as with commercial fish hatcheries, private ponds, and large spring holes (Knudsen andHale 1968, Pearce et al. 2017). Otters have high energetic demands and thus can have significant impacts on food webs (Dekar et al. 2010). Given the economic and cultural significance of trout fishing in West Virginia (Fisher et al. 1998, Southwick Associates 2007, Bell and York 2010), the extent to which otters in West Virginia cause possible economic harm to the sport fishing industry is a critical wildlife management issue.

Despite a substantial scientific effort to reduce the concern that otters are harmful to the trout fishing industry through otter diet composition studies (Lagler and Ostenson 1942, Sheldon and Toll 1964, Knudsen and Hale 1968, Toweill and Tabor 1982, Manning et al. 1990, Heenkenda et al. 2023, Sanders et al. 2023), perceived human-otter conflict persists (Lagler and Ostenson, 1942, Serfass et al. 2014, Pearce et al. 2017). Commercial fish hatcheries are often a primary concern in this conflict. Pearce et al. (2017) determined that in Pennsylvania in 2011, 87% of 156 commercial fish hatcheries reported an annual loss of fish stock from otter depredation amounting to less than 5% of total stock, and 18% of these hatcheries reported an annual loss of fish stock to otters between 5 and 10% of total stock. This study also found that season and landscape characteristics of the fish hatcheries were significant predictors of otter visitation (Pearce et al. 2017). To date, no known study has evaluated otter consumption of stocked fish in private ponds. However, research on the relationships between otter presence in residential areas has concluded that the presence of docks is a significant attractant for river otters (Lesage et al. 2023) which may increase the probability of conflict.

I propose that future research should focus on developing and improving human-otter conflict prevention strategies for the specific circumstances in which humans and otters are known to enter into conflict, i.e., commercial fish hatcheries and private pond s, even if those circumstances are not widespread. Future research could empirically evaluate what measures best prevent human-otter conflict at fish hatcheries and private ponds such as fencing or other deterrents. For example, the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife recommends constructing fencing around such areas that are designed specifically for preventing otters from accessing stocked trout (Link 2005). In a review of non-invasive human-predator conflict prevention strategies, Khorozyan and Waltert (2019) found that electric fencing is the most effective intervention strategy in protecting human assets from predators.

Human-predator conflict is a significant threat to predators worldwide (Ripple et al. 2014, van Eeden et al. 2018), and human-otter conflict is considered one of the primary threats to otter species globally (Duplaix and Savage 2018). Predator removal is often only a short-term solution to human-predator conflict (Lennox et al. 2018). Evidence-based conflict prevention measures have been identified as a critical research need to address predator conservation across the globe (Ripple et al. 2014, Eeden et al. 2018, Lennox et al. 2018, Talbert et al. 2020), including to address human-otter conflict (Duplaix andSavage 2018, Bricker et al. 2022). When empirically based conflict-prevention strategies have been implemented, they have been immensely

successful (van Eeden et al. 2018, Khorozyan andWaltert 2019). Conservation research will need to better integrate human-wildlife conflict prevention programs for predators and humans to coexist (Estes et al. 2011, Ripple et al. 2014).

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Reintroductions (the human-mediated movement of a species into an area of its historic range from which it has been extirpated) are a common tool to restore biodiversity and ecosystem function (IUCN 1987). A reintroduction is considered successful if the reintroduced population is sustainable in the long-term without major human intervention (Griffith et al. 1989). Long-term monitoring is an important component in establishing the success or failure of a reintroduction program (Griffith et al. 1989, Wolf et al. 1996, Schwartz et al. 2007, Frankham 2009), especially because a meta-analysis of 336 reintroduction programs found that most were unsuccessful in establishing self-sustaining populations (Wolf et al. 1996).

The reintroduction of top-order predators is often an important aspect to ecosystem restoration because of their role in ecosystem regulation (Soule et al. 2003, Sergio et al. 2008, Estes et al. 2011, Ripple et al. 2014). Top predators are at higher risk of extinction than other taxa because of life history characteristics such as long generation times, high trophic level, and low population densities (Purvis et al. 2000, Frankham 2009). Reintroductions create the potential for founder effects, which include negative population genetic consequences such as lowered genetic diversity compared to the source population and the potential for inbreeding.

These founder effects are especially threatening to the long-term survival of reintroduced predator populations because of their life history characteristics (Frankham 2009). Inbreeding and lowered genetic diversity can cause reduced immunocompetence, lowered reproductive success, lowered survival rates, and reduced potential for populations to adapt to changing environmental conditions (Armstrong andSeddon 2008, Frankham et al. 2010). Therefore, population genetic monitoring of reintroduced predator populations is imperative for the long-term success of reintroduction programs (DeYoung and Honeycut 2005, Schwartz et al. 2007, Frankham 2009).

The North American river otter (Lontra canadensis, hereafter, otter) was historically present in all major North American watersheds except for the extremities of the Southwestern desert and the Arctic tundra (Hall, 1981;Melquist & Dronkert 1987). However, the onset of European colonization resulted in habitat destruction and unregulated harvest of otters for their fur. By the mid-nineteenth century, otters were extirpated from over 25% of their historic range (Toweill and Tabor 1982, Melquist and Dronkert 1987, Melquist et al. 2003). These extirpations were concentrated in the inland United States, including much of Appalachia, which is attributed to naturally lower prey availability in these habitats compared to coastal areas (Melquist and Dronkert 1987, Melquist et al. 2003, Bricker et al. 2022).

Despite this past, otters are contemporarily considered a conservation success story, including across Appalachia (Raesly 2001, Roberts et al. 2020, Bricker et al. 2022). As of 2016, otters are thought to occupy 90% of their historic range (Duplaix and Savage 2018). This recovery is the result of a synergy of conservation actions that began in the 1970's, namely human-mediated reintroduction programs, watershed restoration, and the implementation of managed harvests (Raesly 2001, Melquist et al. 2003). However, most states that implemented otter reintroduction programs limited their post-reintroduction assessments to the short-term and at the demographic scale. Because otters function as apex predators in Appalachian ecosystems and naturally occur in low densities (Duplaix andSavage 2018, Bricker et al. 2022), they are at higher risk of extinction than other reintroduced species (Purvis et al. 2000, Frankham et al. 2009).

div.head: Sequence Analysis
div.p: The software pipeline STACKS v2.53 (Catchen et al. 2013) was used to filter sequences and identify SNPs. Sequences were cleaned (--clean), barcodes and RAD-Tag cut sites were rescued (--rescue), reads with raw Phred quality scores below 5 were removed (--score 5, -quality), sequences were truncated (-truncate) according to FastQC reports (Andrews 2010), and samples were demultiplexed using process_radtags. Samples with less than 10,000 reads were removed from further analysis. Bowtie2 v2.5.4 (Langmead et al. 2009) was used to align sequences to a Lontra canadensis reference genome (GCF_010015895.1) downloaded from NCBI GenBank. SAMTOOLS was used to convert files from *.sam to *.bam and then to sort *.bam files (Heng et al. 2009). Loci were assembled and population level statistics were calculated using ref_map.pl in STACKS. SNPs had to occur in a minimum of 7 populations (-p 7, out of 8 total populations) and occur in 60% of individuals (-r 0.60) to be kept for further analysis.

div.head: Statistical Analysis-Population Diversity
div.p: Genome-wide expected heterozygosity (genomeHE) was calculated for each sample using Estimates of polymorphic loci, nucleotide diversity, the number of private alleles, observed and expected heterozygosity (HO and HE), the number of loci out of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and the inbreeding coefficient (FIS) were calculated using the populations program in STACKS v2.53 (Catchen et al. 2013). Effective population sizes (Ne) were calculated for each state as well as for each population defined by the population structure analyses. The program NeEstimator (Do et al. 2014) was used for this analysis with the linkage disequilibrium method, assuming random mating and a minimum allele frequency of 0.02. Confidence intervals (95%)

were calculated using parametric estimation. To identify potentially adaptive SNPs, selection analyses were performed using the R packages OutFLANK-0.2 (Whitlock and Lotterhos, 2015) and Pcadapt-4.4.0 (Luu et al., 2016). Only SNPs identified as being potentially under selection by both OutFlank and Pcadapt were considered. The allele frequencies of any potentially adaptive SNPS were compared across populations to assess differences. The functions of these genes were assessed using the nucleotide BLAST tool (BLASTN) using default settings as part of the NCBI platform ( The West Virginia population also had lower estimates of genome-wide heterozygosity than the source populations. This pattern is somewhat unexpected given that the number of founders was relatively high (n = ~248) and similar to the number of founders in states in which the genome-wide heterozygosity estimate was similar to that of the source states (i.e., Ohio, n = 123). Potentially, this pattern is attributed to a synergy of factors including population isolation, low survival of founders, and genetic drift, which could threaten the long-term persistence of this population (Purvis et al. 2000, Frankham 2009). Reintroduction programs of other mammals have found that even with high numbers of founders, adult survival is highly related to the longterm success of reintroductions. In reintroduction programs of western lowland gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla) in Gabon and Congo, a population viability analysis indicated that reintroduction success was highly sensitive to birth rates and adult female survival (King et al. 2013). Similarly, a reintroduction of Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) into France found that reintroduction goals were not met because of low survival of founders (<50%) and population isolation (Vandel et al. 2006). A reintroduction program of Eurasian otters (Lutra lutra) into the Netherlands found that survival was higher for females than males which, in synergy with a polygynous mating system in which only a few males breed, increased the risk of inbreeding and thus reduced the long-term viability of the reintroduced population (Seignobosc et al. 2011). The primary risk of mortality in these reintroductions were human-caused, either roadkill or illegal harvest (Vandel et al. 2006, Seignobosc et al. 2011, King et al. 2013). Potentially, the lower genomic diversity of otters in West Virginia compared to the source population is because of low adult survival despite the high number of founders.
The similar levels of genomic diversity in this study between the reintroduced populations of Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Maryland and the source states (Louisiana and North

Carolina) indicate successful reintroductions. Pennsylvania included several states in their reintroduction program, so even though Louisiana and North Carolina do not perfectly represent source states, they are representative of remnant populations that did not experience extirpations or bottlenecks, and thus still represent a meaningful comparison for genomic diversity.

The selection analyses found five SNPs to be potentially under selection. The differences in allele frequencies of these SNPs were visually examined across the populations. Interestingly, these allele frequencies were fixed in many of the populations except for Ohio-West. Allele frequencies for these SNPs were clearly different in Ohio-West than in the other populations, providing further evidence that this population has ancestry not from the reintroduction program but from populations not sampled in this study (most likely from Michigan). Because of the differences in climate and prey availability between coastal Louisiana and Michigan, these differences in allele frequencies of loci putatively under selection could represent adaptive differences in otters between inland and coastal otters. Unfortunately, because the potential functions of these genes are unknown, I was unable to draw conclusions as to the biological or threshold to prevent the deleterious impacts of inbreeding (Franklin 1980). I recommend that managers prioritize habitat connectivity across this region. Continued genomic monitoring of otters across Ohio will inform the extent to which central Ohio serves as a barrier to gene flow for this species. Increased gene flow across this region could increase genetic diversity for these populations and therefore increase their adaptive potential (Frankham et al. 2010). If additional reintroductions become necessary in the future, alternative source populations should be considered.

Most of these carcasses (n=79) were donated from licensed trappers or damage control agents between the 2020/2021 to the 2022/2023 trapping season (from early November to the end of February). Additional carcasses (n=7) were collected as roadkill or as a result of nuisance permits from outside the trapping season. All otter carcasses were necropsied by the WVDNR, during which the individual's sex, age, county of collection, and means of collection (recreationally trapped, nuisance trapped, or roadkill) were recorded if possible. During necropsies, the entire otter stomach was removed from the carcass by tying both ends with rope and then cutting each end with a scalpel. Entire stomachs were stored individually at -20°C until further analysis. Otter stomachs were later dissected and sub-sampled by thawing them completely and then opening each stomach with a scalpel and placing all contents into a 32-oz glass jar. A paint brush was used to remove the entirety of the stomach contents from the stomach lining. Each stomach was given a relative digestion score between 1 and 4 in accordance with Schnieder et al. (2021) with the modification that 'empty' stomachs were given the 'most digested score' (1). Stomach contents were then homogenized with a stir bar and plate. Once homogenized, approximately 10mL of stomach contents were removed from the mason jar with a serological pipette, placed into a separate collection cup, and stored at -20°C until further analysis. If 10mL were not present in the stomach, as much liquid stomach content as was possible was sub-sampled. The remainder of the stomach contents were used for a concurrent study assessing otter diet composition with microscopy. To prevent contamination, all surfaces and materials were disinfected with bleach and ethanol in between each dissection. All stomach dissections were performed in a PCR-free lab dedicated to sensitive protocols.

The reintroduction history of otters in Ohio partially explains this pattern, as otters were reintroduced only into areas within eastern Ohio. Potentially, western Ohio was naturally recolonized by otters not from the reintroduction but from areas not sampled in this study. The two logical possibilities for this are that otters naturally recolonized western Ohio from Indiana or Michigan. div.head: Chapter 2: Using Conservation Genomics to Assess the Impact of River Otter Reintroductions across Appalachia
div.p: Abstract Appalachian freshwater ecosystems have experienced immense destruction, primarily deforestation and watershed pollution, since European colonization. However, more recently, unprecedented conservation efforts have been applied to restore these ecosystems. North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are apex predators and function as an indicator species, and as such, their conservation is inextricably linked with that of Appalachia. Although otters were extirpated from most of Appalachia by the mid -1900's, watershed restoration and reintroduction programs have allowed this species to return to most of their historic range.

However, an understanding of the population genomic consequences of these reintroductions is needed for contemporary conservation efforts. To address this, I amalgamated otter tissue samples (n=395) collected from 2006-2023 from across several U.S. Appalachian states in which otters were reintroduced (Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia) as well as from the two primary source states for the reintroductions (Louisiana and North Carolina). I analyzed 13,468 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) using a double digest restriction-site (ddRAD) method. These results indicated that two genetically defined populations are present across Appalachia (K=2). Virginia and West Virginia's populations had lower genome-wide heterozygosity measures than the source states and effective population sizes were low across the study area (Ne < 500). These data will guide conservation decision-makers as to how to best ensure the long-term persistence of this species. These results are also informative as to Appalachian ecosystem recovery progress.

Reintroduced otter populations are also at risk of negative founder effects because most of the otter reintroduction programs selected source otter populations based solely on their accessibility, and few of these programs (36%) considered population genetics or subspecies information (Raesly 2001). Over 4,000 otters were translocated across the United States during otter reintroduction programs in the late 1900s and early 2000's. The majority (64%) of translocated otters were sourced from Louisiana, oftentimes because this population has historically remained abundant (Ralls 1990, Raesly 2001). Although this source population has succeeded from a demographic standpoint in establishing reintroduced populations across the United States, the population genetic impacts of this process are unknown (Raesly 2001, Roberts et al. 2020, Bricker et al. 2022). Landscape genetic research on otters in Louisiana identified three distinct populations within the state, which was unexpected given the abundance of aquatic habitat statewide and lack of perceived barriers to dispersal across the state (Latch et al. 2008).

Potentially these populations are distinct as a result of either differences in prey availability or a correlation between freshwater access across inland and coastal habitats (Latch et al. 2008). No records exist as to which of these three subpopulations constituted most translocated otters, but potential adaptive differences between coastal and inland otter populations could have implications for reintroduction success (Latch et al. 2008, Serfass et al. 1998).

Although much remains to be discovered about the population genetic-scale impacts of otter reintroductions across North America, most initial research to this end has found evidence that reintroduced otter populations retain genetic diversity and structure similar to source populations (Brandt et al. 2014, Mowry et al. 2011). Across central North America, otter populations exhibited high levels of genetic diversity, similar to source populations, indicating their resiliency as a species (Brandt et al. 2014). Within this region, a reintroduced population in South Dakota exhibited similarly high levels of heterozygosity as a naturally recolonized population in North Dakota, further providing evidence for the success of these initiatives (Brandt et al. 2014). In Missouri, the reintroduced otter population exhibited population diversity and structure representative of the source population (Louisiana), indicating that the reintroduction was successful at the population genetics scale (Mowry et al. 2011). This pattern of recovery from population reduction is potentially because of the high dispersal capacity of this species (Melquist and Hornocker 1983). The only study to-date that has found significant founder effects in a reintroduced population, and therefore a potentially unsuccessful reintroduction, was in New Mexico, but this is most likely attributed to a small founder population size (n=33; Murphy et al. 2021). However, the above studies all utilized microsatellites, which assess non-coding regions of the genome, and therefore cannot be used to understand adaptive or selective patterns in these populations. Further research on the population genomic impacts of the otter reintroduction program, including an understanding of adaptive or selective patterns, has been identified as a research need for otter conservation and management across North America (Duplaix andSavage 2018, Bricker et al. 2022).

Across Appalachia, otters were widely extirpated by the mid -1900s. Reintroduction programs began in the 1980's and continued into the early 2000's. The reintroduction projects of the states included in this study are summarized in Table 1, but most translocated otters were sourced from Louisiana (Raesly 2001, Roberts et al. 2020, Bricker et al. 2022). These reintroductions were mostly considered successful by the 2010's, and as a result, trapping seasons were opened in many states between 2010 and 2015. However, the reintroductions were deemed successful without an assessment of population genomics (Bricker et al. 2022).

To address this issue, in this chapter, I will evaluate the population genomic impacts of otters across five Appalachian states (Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia) and two source states (Louisiana and North Carolina) using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), a genomic method. This research will provide valuable assessments of the current status of reintroduced populations from a population genomics perspective. Wildlife managers will be informed as to the extent to which the reintroduction programs captured sufficient genomic diversity to secure the long-term persistence of these populations. Best management practices can then be implemented to balance the needs of ecosystem conservation and human uses. This is also the first study to utilize a genomic method, as opposed to genetic methods, to assess river otter reintroductions, which will be informative as to adaptive and selective differences in this species overall. This research will contribute to the long-term goal of conserving West Virginia's reintroduced river otter population for both the purposes of ecological functioning (as apex predators) and as a resource for human uses (as a trapped furbearer). I hypothesize that the reintroduction programs were successful in securing the longterm persistence of the reintroduced populations. If the reintroduction programs were successful in securing the long-term persistence of the reintroduced populations, the reintroduced population will exhibit genomic diversity similar to the source populations. I formulated this hypothesis based on published research that has found high levels of genetic diversity in reintroduced otter populations elsewhere in the United States (Mowry et al. 2011, Brandt et al. 2014).

div.head: Population Diversity
div.p: Genome-wide heterozygosity measures showed that Virginia and West Virginia had lower heterozygosity levels than their source states, Louisiana and North Carolina (Figure 5).
All other states had genome-wide heterozygosity levels overlapping with the source states.

Virginia had the highest inbreeding coefficients (Table 2). Virginia had the lowest number of private alleles, nucleotide diversity, observed heterozygosity (HO), and a low effective population size (Ne = 7.4, 95% CI's = 5.9-9.0; Table 2).

In Pcadapt and OutFLANK identified five SNPs as being potentially under selection, representing 0.04% of total SNPs analyzed (Figure 6). Out of those five SNPs, only one was correspond to differences in habitat types (primarily coastal versus inland habitats; Latch et al. 2008). The genetic structuring observed in Louisiana is thought to persist because of differences in prey availability which affects dispersal distances and social organizations (Latch et al. 2008).
Future research should investigate to what extent barriers exist to gene flow for otters across Ohio.

div.head: Population Diversity
div.p: The population diversity analyses overall provide evidence that the populations in Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Maryland have genomic diversity similar to the source states of Louisiana and North Carolina and that Virginia and West Virginia have lower genomic d iversity than the source states. This result is somewhat surprising given the difference in the number of founders between Virginia (n=17) and West Virginia (n=~248). The varying success of otter reintroductions elsewhere is thought to be a result of differences in the number of founders. In Missouri, 800 otters were translocated, and the reintroduced otter population was found to have heterozygosity levels similar to the source state (Louisiana; Mowry et al. 2015). In South Dakota, only 34 otters were translocated, and the reintroduced otter population had lower heterozygosity than the source state (Louisiana; Brandt et al. 2013). Founder effects are known to have significant impacts on reintroduced predator populations (Armstrong andSeddon 2008, Frankham 2009), but do not explain the low genomic diversity observed in the reintroduced West Virginia population given the high number of founders.

The Virginia population had the lowest estimate of genome-wide heterozygosity, nucleotide diversity, private alleles, and observed heterozygosity, as well as a low effective population size (Ne = 7.4, 95% CI's = 5.9-9.0). This pattern is not unexpected given that the Virginia reintroduction program had the lowest number of founders (n=17, compared to between ecological significance of these differences. However, adaptive differences have been identified

from SNPs and loci putatively under selection in populations of bats in different climatic conditions (Razgour et al. 2017), in different evolutionary lineages of mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus; Powell et al. 2016), and in mountain hares (Lepus timidus) across distinct habitats (Giska et al. 2021). Adaptive differences have also been identified from SNPs in reintroduction and recolonization events. A reintroduction of Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) into a habitat with longer migration routes in Washington, USA found loci to be putatively under selection in genes that code for functions related to migration fitness in the reintroduced population (Campbell et al. 2017). Future research should investigate to what extent the loci identified here as putatively under selection in otters represent adaptive differences between inland and coastal otters. These differences could impact adaptive potential for otters across the continent as climates change.

div.head: Management Implications
div.p: This study provides evidence that the otter reintroduction programs across Appalachia were successful in that most reintroduced populations have shared ancestry to the source states and most populations have similar levels of genomic diversity to the source populations.

However, Virginia and West Virginia have lower levels of genome-wide heterozygosity than the source states, which may have negative implications for the long-term persistence of those populations. This study also provides evidence that the reintroduced otter populations in central Appalachia are isolated from populations to the West and East. Some of the effective population sizes estimates (Ne) for these populations were below 500, which is considered a threshold to represent the minimum Ne to ensure long-term population viability (Franklin 1980). div.head: Management Implications
div.p: The results of the diet study described here provide evidence that otters in West Virginia do not consume species of trout as a main diet item. I recommend that managers focus on developing and improving human-otter conflict prevention strategies for the specific circumstances in which humans and otters are known to enter into conflict, i.e., commercial fish hatcheries and private ponds, even if those circumstances are not widespread. Future research could empirically evaluate what measures best prevent human-otter conflict at fish hatcheries and private ponds such as fencing or other deterrents. I also recommend that managers prioritize education and outreach initiatives to better disseminate these results.

The results of the population genomics study described here provide evidence that the reintroduction program was largely successful in restoring otter populations in West Virginia as well as across Appalachia. I recommend that managers incorporate increasing levels of gene flow across the landscape with the goal of increasing genomic diversity and thus adaptive potential for this species to ensure their long-term persistence across Appalachia. Specifically, restoring connectivity across the state of Ohio could introduce novel, adaptive genes to the population which could increase genomic diversity and adaptive potential for otters across Appalachia. If future reintroductions were necessary, alternative source populations should be evaluated.
